title: 6.1 — Hat Matrix, Residual Maker and Quadratic Forms
breadcrumb: Unit VI → Regression and linear models → 6.1 Hat matrix, residual maker and quadratic forms
engineName: Derive the OLS projection and residual operators, then use their matrix properties to solve regression questions.
objectives: Derive the hat matrix H and residual-maker matrix M from the OLS projection.
Prove that H and M are symmetric and idempotent under full-column-rank OLS.
Use H and M to express fitted values, residuals, SSE and residual orthogonality.
Connect trace and rank of projection matrices to model and residual degrees of freedom.
Evaluate quadratic forms involving symmetric idempotent matrices.
Avoid confusing the hat matrix, residual maker, projection space and their ranks.

traps: H projects y onto C(X), while M projects y onto the orthogonal complement of C(X).
H and M are both symmetric and idempotent; M=I−H.
rank(H)=trace(H)=k when X has full column rank k; rank(M)=trace(M)=n−k.
The diagonal entries hᵢᵢ are leverage values; they are not generally all equal.
The residual vector is e=My and satisfies X′e=0.
For a symmetric idempotent matrix A, y′Ay is nonnegative and has rank(A) degrees of freedom under a standard normal vector.

sheet: H=X(X′X)⁻¹X′ is the hat matrix; ŷ=Hy.
M=I−H is the residual-maker matrix; e=My.
H′=H and H²=H; M′=M and M²=M.
X′M=0, so X′e=0 and residuals are orthogonal to every column of X.
For symmetric idempotent A, y′Ay≥0; if y~N(0,σ²I), y′Ay/σ² has χ²_rank(A) distribution.
hᵢᵢ are leverages, 0≤hᵢᵢ≤1 and sum hᵢᵢ=k.
M removes the fitted component and leaves the residual component.
tricks: To prove H²=H, cancel X′X between the two factors using (X′X)⁻¹X′X=I.
For M², expand (I−H)² and use H²=H.
Trace is invariant under cyclic rearrangement: tr(ABC)=tr(BCA) when dimensions conform.
For idempotent matrices, eigenvalues are 0 or 1, so trace equals rank.
shortcuts: H keeps the component in C(X); M removes it.
Trace equals rank for symmetric idempotent projection matrices.
remember: These formulas assume X has full column rank for the ordinary inverse expression.
For rank-deficient X, projection onto C(X) still exists, but use a suitable generalized inverse; do not blindly use (X′X)⁻¹.

scenes.title: Refresh the matrix tools
scenes.objective: Rebuild the algebra used to derive projection matrices.
body: This lesson is built around two matrices: one keeps the fitted part of the response, and the other keeps the residual part. Their properties come from ordinary matrix algebra.
You do not need to memorise every identity at once. First recover transpose, inverse, rank and orthogonality; then each result will follow from a short calculation.

items.ask: What is the transpose of a product AB?
refresh: A transpose exchanges rows and columns. For a matrix A, the entry in row i and column j moves to row j and column i.
For products, the order reverses: (AB)′=B′A′. This is why the transpose of X(X′X)⁻¹X′ can be simplified by transposing each factor and reversing the order.
The matrix X′X is symmetric because (X′X)′=X′X. Its inverse is also symmetric, which is used in proving H′=H.
When proving matrix identities, preserve factor order. Associativity lets you regroup adjacent factors, but matrices cannot generally be swapped.

items.ask: If X has full column rank k, what can you say about X′X?
refresh: Full column rank means none of the k columns of X is a linear combination of the others.
For any nonzero a, a′X′Xa=(Xa)′(Xa)=||Xa||². Full column rank ensures Xa is not zero, so this quantity is positive.
Therefore X′X is positive definite and invertible. This is the condition behind the ordinary OLS formula β̂=(X′X)⁻¹X′y.
If the design is rank deficient, the projection onto C(X) still exists, but the ordinary inverse formula must be replaced by a suitable generalized-inverse treatment.

items.ask: What does it mean for two vectors to be orthogonal?
refresh: The inner product of two real column vectors a and b is a′b. They are orthogonal when this scalar equals zero.
A vector is orthogonal to a subspace when it is orthogonal to every vector in that subspace. In regression, the residual is orthogonal to every column of X.
Writing this condition for all columns at once gives X′e=0. These are the OLS normal equations in residual form.
Orthogonality also explains why fitted and residual components form perpendicular projections of y.

ask.q: Which matrix operation reverses factor order when transposing a product?
ask.nudge: Recall the transpose rule for AB.

scenes.title: Fitted part and leftover part
body: OLS chooses the fitted vector ŷ inside the column space of X. The residual e=y−ŷ is the part of y left over after projection onto that space.
The hat matrix H maps y to ŷ. The residual-maker matrix M maps y to e. They split the same response vector into two perpendicular components: y=Hy+My.
Think of H as keeping the model-explained component and M as removing it.

scenario.teaser: Project a data vector onto a model space
scenario.title: Two operators, one decomposition
body: Suppose the columns of X span all fitted vectors that the regression model can produce. OLS selects the point in that space closest to y.
The projection operator H produces that fitted point. The remaining perpendicular vector is the residual, produced by M=I−H.

Because the fitted and residual components are orthogonal, their inner product is zero. The total squared length of y splits into fitted and residual sums of squares when the model includes the appropriate intercept/centering convention.
This geometry is the foundation for the algebraic properties tested in NET questions.
scenario.q: Which matrix produces the residual vector from y?

ask.q: What is the relationship between the fitted and residual components?
ask.nudge: They add to y and are perpendicular.

scenes.title: Derive the hat matrix
scenes.objective: Obtain H from the OLS estimator.
body: For y=Xβ+u, the full-column-rank OLS estimator is β̂=(X′X)⁻¹X′y. The fitted vector is ŷ=Xβ̂.
Substitute the estimator into the fitted vector: ŷ=X(X′X)⁻¹X′y. The matrix multiplying y is called the hat matrix H.
Therefore H=X(X′X)⁻¹X′ and ŷ=Hy. It is n×n because it maps an n-vector y to another n-vector ŷ.

viz.caption: The hat matrix projects the response vector onto the column space of X.

ask.q: What is the dimension of H when X is n×k?
ask.nudge: H maps an n-dimensional response vector to an n-dimensional fitted vector.

scenario.teaser: A response vector is projected onto a model space
scenario.title: Why the hat matrix is a projection
body: Imagine that the columns of X span a plane of all fitted vectors the regression can produce. The observed response y may not lie in that plane.
OLS chooses the point in the plane that is closest to y in squared Euclidean distance. That point is the fitted vector, and H maps y to it.
The leftover difference is perpendicular to the plane. The residual-maker matrix M maps y to that perpendicular component.
This geometry tells us what H and M do before we calculate their algebraic properties.
scenario.q: What does H return when it acts on y?
scenario.answer: The orthogonal projection of y onto the column space of X, namely the fitted vector.

scenes.title: Symmetry and idempotence of H
scenes.objective: Prove the two defining projection properties.

blocks.body: H′=[X(X′X)⁻¹X′]′=X[(X′X)⁻¹]′X′=X(X′X)⁻¹X′=H, since X′X and its inverse are symmetric.
A projection performed twice has the same result as performing it once. Once y is in C(X), projecting it onto C(X) again does not move it.

scenes.objective: Simplify H² without skipping matrix order.

steps.say: Write the product H times H, preserving the factor order.
steps.why: Matrix multiplication is associative but not commutative.
The middle product is the matrix being inverted.

steps.why: The product equals H, which proves idempotence.

ask.q: What property of matrix multiplication must you not assume in this proof?
ask.nudge: You may regroup factors, but you cannot freely swap their order.

scenes.title: Ranks, traces and degrees of freedom
scenes.objective: Use projection dimension to obtain model and residual degrees of freedom.

blocks.body: If rank(X)=k, then rank(H)=k and tr(H)=k.
M=I−H projects onto a space of dimension n−k, so rank(M)=tr(M)=n−k.
The residual sum of squares has n−k residual degrees of freedom under the standard full-rank linear model.

ask.q: If n=30 and k=4, what are tr(H) and tr(M)?
ask.nudge: The two projection-space dimensions add to n.

scenes.title: Orthogonality and the residual vector
scenes.objective: Show that residuals are orthogonal to the design columns.
body: Since M=I−H and H projects onto C(X), the residual component is perpendicular to every column of X. Algebraically, X′M=0.
Thus e=My implies X′e=X′My=0. This is exactly the OLS normal-equation condition.
The fitted and residual projection matrices are mutually annihilating: HM=MH=0. Also H+M=I.

viz.caption: The fitted space and residual space are orthogonal complements when X has full column rank.

ask.q: What matrix equation expresses residual orthogonality to all columns of X?

scenes.problem: Let X=1₃, a three-entry column of ones. Find H and M.

steps.why: The design has one column and three observations.
The projection replaces each observation by the sample mean.
The residual maker removes the fitted constant component.

steps.why: The residuals are deviations from the sample mean and sum to zero.

ask.q: What is the rank of this intercept-only hat matrix?
ask.nudge: Its column space is the one-dimensional span of the vector of ones.

scenes.objective: Calculate model and residual degrees of freedom.
scenes.problem: A regression has n=24 observations and k=5 linearly independent columns in X. Find rank(H), tr(H), rank(M), tr(M) and residual degrees of freedom.
hints: The fitted space has dimension k.
The residual space is the orthogonal complement, with dimension n−k.
For symmetric idempotent projection matrices, trace equals rank.
scenes.answer: rank(H)=tr(H)=5; rank(M)=tr(M)=19; residual degrees of freedom=19.

solution.say: The hat matrix projects onto C(X).
For a projection matrix, trace equals rank.
The residual space has dimension n−k.
Trace and residual degrees of freedom match that dimension.

ask.q: Why is residual df not n−1 in this model?
ask.nudge: There are five independent fitted directions, not just one.

scenes.title: Exam traps: H, M and rank
scenes.intro: Classify each statement as true or false.

items.claim: H is always k×k when X is n×k.
items.why: H maps n-vectors to n-vectors, so it is n×n.

items.claim: Both H and M are idempotent.
tr(H)=k when X has full column rank k.
items.why: The projection onto C(X) has dimension k.
OLS residuals are orthogonal to the column space of X.

hints: Use the transpose rule and M′=M.
Use M²=M to reduce the product.

solution.why: The quadratic form in M equals the residual sum of squares.

ask.nudge: One handles the transpose; the other collapses the repeated matrix.

scenes.title: Summary: projection matrix toolkit
scenes.objective: Recall the identities used in NET/JRF problems.
body: H=X(X′X)⁻¹X′ is the n×n hat matrix and ŷ=Hy. It is symmetric and idempotent. M=I−H is the residual maker and e=My; it too is symmetric and idempotent.
The projections are complementary: H+M=I and HM=MH=0. With rank(X)=k, rank(H)=tr(H)=k and rank(M)=tr(M)=n−k. Residuals satisfy X′e=0.
For the residual sum of squares, e′e=y′M′My=y′My. In quadratic-form questions, use symmetry and idempotence before expanding entries.

ask.q: State the two most important properties shared by H and M.
ask.nudge: One concerns transpose; the other concerns squaring the matrix.
